items.summary:
Apple has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and former Apple employees, accusing them of stealing trade secrets related to unreleased technologies and confidential information. The lawsuit names Chang Liu and Tang Tan, former Apple engineers now at OpenAI, alleging they used insider knowledge to gain further confidential information during job interviews and directed candidates to bring Apple hardware components for evaluation.

The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, claims Apple raised concerns with OpenAI in February but received no response. Apple alleges that OpenAI's hardware business, led by former Apple design chief Jony Ive, benefits from this misappropriated information. The lawsuit highlights coordinated efforts at multiple levels within OpenAI to acquire Apple's confidential data.

items.title: Report: Corporate America faces productivity challenges from overreliance on AI-generated content, creating 'slop zombies' who produce excessive, low-quality work [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rise of the 'Slop Zombies'
items.summary:
A recent analysis highlights a growing issue in corporate America where employees excessively depend on AI chatbots to generate detailed but often low-quality reports, emails, and presentations. This overuse leads to a phenomenon dubbed 'slop zombies,' characterized by diminished critical thinking, inflated confidence, and reduced productivity as workers rely heavily on AI outputs without sufficient oversight or understanding.

The report describes how this reliance creates a feedback loop where employees produce verbose AI-generated content that others must then simplify, further spreading inefficiency. It also notes that many managers have adopted this approach, mandating widespread AI use, which devalues human feedback and social skills. The distinction between effective AI users and 'slop zombies' lies in the ability to critically evaluate and modify AI outputs, a skill many affected workers lack, resulting in cognitive decline and workplace challenges.

The article examines a mathematical model developed by researchers Brett Hemenway Falk and Gerry Tsoukalas that explains how AI-driven automation can lead to layoffs, which in turn reduce consumer demand and harm companies' overall performance. This dynamic creates a competitive dilemma where firms feel pressured to automate to avoid falling behind, even if the collective outcome is negative.

The model considers two competing companies deciding whether to adopt AI automation, weighing potential cost savings against losses from decreased consumer spending due to layoffs. If automation savings are less than the demand loss, both firms automating results in worse outcomes for both. This scenario helps explain the paradox of rising stock markets alongside increasing job insecurity in the AI industry, contributing to economic anxiety despite strong market indicators.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI’s Head of Safety Is Leaving the Company
items.summary:
Johannes Heidecke, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, is departing the company following a reorganization that merges safety and research teams under VP Mia Glaese. The change aims to better coordinate safety efforts as OpenAI accelerates model training and release cycles.

Mark Chen, OpenAI’s chief research officer, announced that safety teams will now report to Glaese, who will serve as VP of research and safety, with Saachi Jain stepping in as interim head of safety systems. Heidecke joined OpenAI in 2021 and became head of safety systems in 2024 after Lilian Weng's departure.

Heidecke’s exit coincides with OpenAI’s launch of GPT-5.6, its most capable model yet, which exhibited some concerning misaligned behaviors. Other recent leadership changes include the departure of chief futurist Joshua Achiam and CEO of AGI deployment Fidji Simo stepping down after medical leave, with Greg Brockman taking on expanded product and go-to-market responsibilities.

items.originalTitle: Hermes – AI that turns customer behavior into actions instead of dashboards
items.summary:
Hermes offers an AI-driven platform that analyzes product data, billing, CRM, and support tickets to identify customer activation blockers, churn risks, and expansion opportunities, then automatically drafts and routes personalized emails, alerts, and tasks. The system integrates with tools like HubSpot, Salesforce, Slack, Linear, and Jira, enabling teams to act on insights with one click and improve customer engagement without manual dashboard analysis.

The platform builds a dynamic customer map by connecting to data sources via a read-only Postgres connection, continuously learning from approvals and edits to refine its actions. Hermes emphasizes data privacy by processing customer data in memory without storing it, allowing users to delete data at any time. Early users report significant improvements in activation rates and customer understanding through automated, behavior-driven interventions.

items.originalSummary:
In the months ahead of Apple’s lawsuit against OpenAI on Friday, the iPhone maker’s concerns about OpenAI’s plans to compete in consumer hardware have mounted steadily.

For starters, there was the seemingly never-ending stream of Apple employees jumping ship to join the AI startup. As those departures began to reach into the hundreds, Apple scrambled to make counteroffers to employees being recruited by OpenAI with more compensation and additional job responsibilities, said people familiar with the matter.

Apple’s frustration with the outflow of employees came to a head in the lawsuit, which accused the AI startup of a “systematic effort” to steal Apple trade secrets to develop its own AI-powered devices for consumers. The lawsuit says that OpenAI has recruited more than 400 former Apple employees to work at the company and names two Apple alumni as defendants: Tang Tan, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, and Chang Liu, a member of OpenAI’s technical staff.

items.originalTitle: I run my agency's 10 AI agents from launchd, no n8n, 0 dependencies
items.summary:
A developer manages their agency's operations through 10 AI agents scheduled via launchd, avoiding frameworks like n8n and dependencies such as Docker. Each agent is a single Node.js file with unit-tested guardrails that prevent unsafe or irreversible actions, ensuring controlled execution. The system includes features like allowlists, do-not-contact lists, deduplication, and daily caps to maintain safety and compliance.

The project is open-sourced as a clean template on GitHub, featuring a pure function to evaluate proposed actions before execution, with safe defaults that prevent sending emails without explicit opt-in. It supports scheduling on macOS, Linux, and cron, and includes examples for email follow-ups and Slack-style digests. The repository also contains unit tests and continuous integration for Node.js versions 18, 20, and 22.

items.title: How ‘Eggmaxing’ Became the Latest Fertility Quest
items.originalTitle: How ‘Eggmaxing’ Became the Latest Fertility Quest
items.summary:
Among the many private group chats circulating through Silicon Valley these days, one of the more unusual ones is a thread called “To Make an Omelette.”

The chat, which was started last year, numbers more than 80 women, including tech founders and other white-collar professionals. (It was originally assembled by Aella, a figure within the Bay Area’s AI rationalist scene, who is also a pseudonymous sex worker.) I spoke with several “To Make an Omelette” participants, most of whom did not want to share their identities publicly given the sensitive topic of the group’s conversation: female fertility—and how they can produce more eggs.

The women, mainly in their 20s and 30s, join because they are freezing their eggs or planning for it. The procedure is a linchpin of fertility treatments such as in vitro fertilization, which now accounts for more than 2% of births in the U.S. every year.

Doctors usually advise women under 35 that they should plan for one to two rounds of egg freezing to harvest 15 eggs, a number that offers good odds of having one child. “To Make an Omelette” emerged to support women who are banking—or at least attempting to bank—dozens and dozens of eggs, perhaps 100 or more. They belong to a niche but growing community of women—call them eggmaxxers.

items.title: How to Conduct a Competitive Analysis with Google Gemini [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to Conduct a Competitive Analysis with Google Gemini
items.summary:
Decisions about when, where, and how to expand a business are always fraught with uncertainty. The prospect of growing the business and reaching new customers with novel offerings is enticing, but a false step can be extremely costly.

A well-researched competitive analysis can reduce this risk by surfacing potential stumbling blocks at the very beginning of the brainstorming process. Historically, these analyses have been extremely time-consuming, as they have required business leaders to manually look through hundreds of pages of annual reports, painstakingly track competitor pricing, and synthesize consumer sentiment from social media and review websites.

With Gemini, organizations can quickly generate an initial competitive analysis report, helping leaders decide whether a new venture is worth pursuing.

Step 1: Prompt Gemini

To get the best results, you’ll want to be as specific as possible. Consider using a prompt that gives Gemini a persona and a clear objective, which will help ensure that Gemini approaches the task from the viewpoint of a business leader, rather than a casual searcher. Here’s an example:

I am a CMO conducting a competitive analysis. My company is considering expanding into [a new line of business]. Generate a list of the top five competitors in the [industry] industry and include their pricing, strengths, weaknesses, and target audience.

If you type your prompt into the “Ask Gemini” box, Gemini will return a high-level briefing in just a few seconds. If you want something more comprehensive, click on the “Tools” button and select “Deep Research,” then run your prompt. Gemini will create a research plan. Review the plan, suggest any needed tweaks, and then click “Start Research.”

For a Deep Research report, Gemini will produce a competitive analysis with citations and sources.

Step 2: Interrogate the Output

Gemini’s initial response or report should be treated as a starting point, not a finished analysis. While the model can quickly surface competitors, pricing models, and positioning, you still need to use your own industry and market expertise to evaluate and refine those insights.

First, simply check to make sure that Gemini’s output aligns with your knowledge of the space. Is the list of competitors complete, or are any key players missing? Does the pricing reflect what you’ve seen in the real world?

Ask Gemini to fill in any gaps. You might go back and forth several times, with each response containing more complete and nuanced information. This iterative process helps ensure that Gemini delivers the exact details you need to determine how to move forward.

Step 3: Create a Five-Year Plan

Once you have a clearer picture of the competitive landscape, you can begin to map out a strategic direction. Here again, Gemini can get you started. Try this sample prompt:

Okay, I am going to try to convince my CEO that we should expand into [line of business]. Draft a concise, competitive strategy outline for the next five years for the [industry] industry across North American markets with potential goals, strategies, and tactics.

You can also add any relevant sources so Gemini has more information about your organization. Gemini’s plan may include initial goals for market penetration, specific tactics to support strategic pillars, and a year-by-year execution roadmap. Just as with the competitive analysis report, you should bring your own judgment and expertise to this five-year plan. Build on what you find helpful, and push back on areas that feel weak or impractical.

Keep working with Gemini until you have an outline that is both realistic and aligned with your goals.

Step 4: Make the Work Your Own

Before presenting your expansion plan to leadership, revise it to include essential details that aren’t included in Gemini’s training data: your internal capabilities, budget constraints, existing customer relationships, and leadership priorities.

Replace any generic language with details grounded in your market knowledge, and adjust timelines or tactics based on what your team can realistically execute. You may also want to incorporate case studies or data points from your company’s previous efforts to strengthen your case.

With Gemini, you can complete the comprehensive background work needed for an expansion effort that succeeds in the real world.

items.summary:
The AI laggards are going on the offensive! Meta Platforms on Thursday unveiled its latest AI model, Muse Spark 1.1, a day after SpaceX’s AI unit introduced a new model of its own. Like SpaceX, Meta claimed its new model delivers performance comparable to that of established models from AI labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. We’ll have to wait a few days to see whether developers agree. (Meanwhile, OpenAI unveiled its latest models, GPT 5.6).

What may be most significant, however, is Meta’s apparent intention to spend a fortune subsidizing usage of its new model in hopes of pulling market share from its rivals. In an interview with Bloomberg, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta’s pricing for what users would pay to use the models would be “very aggressive and attractive.” Bloomberg’s report said Meta’s prices would be about a quarter of those advertised by top models from Anthropic and OpenAI—in other words, dirt cheap.

items.originalTitle: Cursor Is Developing an AI Agent to Compete With Claude Cowork
items.summary:
Cursor is developing a general-purpose AI agent meant to compete with popular tools like Anthropic’s Claude Cowork, two people familiar with the project said, part of a broader push by the company to diversify beyond coding-focused tools.

Work on the new agent began after Cursor started leasing compute capacity in April from SpaceX’s AI unit, known as SpaceXAI, the people said, and comes ahead of SpaceX’s planned $60 billion acquisition of Cursor. The new agent could buttress the enterprise business of SpaceX’s AI unit once that deal closes. It follows the two companies’ joint introduction of a new model, Grok 4.5, meant to perform engineering tasks as well as general knowledge work.
